$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t).

$$

For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1-(-1) & 0 \\ 3 & -1-(-1)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 3{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

q-33233.source_problem:
The equations of a curve $r(t)$ and its corresponding unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at an arbitrary point are given below. Find the principal normal vector to that curve at the point $P(0,3,4).$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k,\,t\in [0,2\pi ) \\ T(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k,\,t\in [0,2\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,3,4)$ on the given curve. We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,3,4⟩ \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k & =0\text{ }i+3\text{ }j+4\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components of $i$, $j$, and $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{cos}⁡t=0 \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t=3 \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t=4\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,3,4)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

Anna is an environmentalist and is studying the impact of deforestation in a pine forest located in a square-shaped region. Anna discovers that the area of ​​the deforested region is decreasing at a rate of $0.4{\text{ km}}^{2}/\text{month}.$ At what rate are the region's diagonals decreasing if the diagonals are $20\text{ km}$ long?
q-48372.worked_solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{h}\cdot \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $A$ decreases at a rate of $0.4{\text{ km}}^{2}/\text{month},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the diagonals when the diagonal has length $h=20.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{20}\cdot (-0.4) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{0.4}{20} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-0.02\,\text{km}\text{/month}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the diagonals of the region are decreasing at a rate of  $0.02\text{ km}/\text{month}.$
